title: feat(refinement-list): Move default template to its own file
body:
I've moved the default template from inline inside the widget to its
own file.

This will make my work adding the CSS classes much easier as I will
now have separate js, html and css files. As a bonus I gain syntax
highlighting and linters in vim as well.

I also think this will make generating the documentation (with HTML
code examples of the default templates) easier.

@vvo pointed out that `require`-ing html files was more or less
a webpack-specific feature and would be hard to port to other build
system. I feel that it's still worth it; what are your thoughts?

comments.body:
I would do like the hits widgets does: https://github.com/algolia/instantsearch.js/blob/develop/widgets/hits/defaultTemplates.js

Mostly because we will be able to get rid of the mighty webpack loaders that are a pain to handle and bad for portability to our users (i.e. using require(instantsearch.js))

With templatestrings and regular js files you are good I think. Those templates are really small.
Sure thing, let's keep the standard way to require stuff. I've upated the branch. I will lose the highlight/linter but those templates are really small so I can live with that.
seems like the commit message check do not allow dashes in the (scope). We can fix that. But here you can also have (refinementList) because that's the real name of the widget API.
(we still need to fix the commit message validator :))

> seems like the commit message check do not allow dashes in the (scope).

It does, probably something else but I don't get it right now: https://github.com/algolia/instantsearch.js/blob/develop/scripts/validate-commit-msgs.sh#L38
I've rebased and forced pushed back. Travis is happy this time :)
Yes we need to put them in defaultTemplates.js as the Hits widget is doing. Otherwise using our lib in a clean way using browserify or webpack will be a pain.

With template strings it's really easy to do templates multiline. It does not depend on any module loader, we are compatible with any JavaScript environment.

Webpack loaders/browserify transforms are cool hacks but then you are tied to the module loader.
